result.target_topic: Impact of Interest Rates on FTP and Margins
result.target_summary: Higher average interest rates increased the cost of funds for assets and FTP benefit for liabilities, leading to higher funding costs for loans and Markets activities and deposit margin compression as rates paid to depositors increased more than the FTP benefit.

target_year_over_year_context.explanation: Both disclosures analyze the impact of the interest rate environment on the FTP process and segment net interest income. D101 (2023) describes how higher rates increased cost of funds and contributed to margin expansion on deposits. D094 (2024) describes how higher average rates increased cost of funds but resulted in deposit margin compression because rates paid to depositors increased more than the FTP benefit. They share the specific topic of FTP-driven NII sensitivity to rate changes.

comparisons.peer_summary: Net interest income decreased $1.4 billion to $13.2 billion primarily due to higher deposit costs and lower average loan balances, partially offset by higher average deposit balances.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and BAC identify higher interest rates and resulting higher deposit costs as a key driver impacting net interest income and margins. JPM explicitly states that higher average rates increased the cost of funds for loans and Markets activities, and that rates paid to depositors increased more than the FTP benefit, causing deposit margin compression. Similarly, BAC attributes its net interest income decrease to higher deposit costs, illustrating a shared exposure to margin compression from rising rate environments despite differences in their net interest income outcomes (JPM notes the mechanism, BAC reports the aggregate decrease).

sentences.text: As a result of higher average interest rates, the cost of funds for assets and the FTP benefit earned for liabilities have generally increased in the current year, impacting the net interest income of the business segments.
During the period ended December 31, 2024, this has resulted in a higher cost of funds for loans and Markets activities.
In addition, rates paid to deposit holders increased more than the FTP benefit increase during the year, resulting in deposit margin compression.
Net interest income decreased $1.4 billion to $13.2 billion primarily due to higher deposit costs and lower average loan balances, partially offset by the benefit of higher average deposit balances.

comparisons.comparison: Both companies disclose that higher average interest rates drove up interest expense on liabilities, impacting net interest income dynamics. JPM details this through the Funds Transfer Pricing (FTP) lens, noting higher funding costs for assets and loans due to higher rates. GS similarly attributes its increase in interest expense to higher average interest rates on liabilities, specifically citing collateralized financings and deposits. Both confirm that the higher rate environment directly increased the cost of funds.
